title: AI Safety Coverage Map

levels.area: A broad part of AI safety research, such as Alignment.
levels.problem: A specific research question inside an area, such as scalable oversight.
levels.approach: A method that can serve problems in several areas, such as debate.

states.covered: Read in depth: the key papers read in full, with records, open questions and later work tracked.
states.partly: Some sources in the atlas (abstracts, quoted passages, code or Lean proofs), but no systematic sweep.

rules: Three levels. A research area is a broad part of safety, a research problem is a specific question inside it, and an approach is a method that can serve problems in several areas.
Version 3 was checked against the 2026 Singapore Consensus on Global AI Safety Research Priorities and the MIT AI Risk Repository's risk domains. Entries added in version 3 are marked new.
Problems carry the marks. An area counts as covered only when all its problems are, and as partly covered when any of them has a source.
Some problems list what they include. Those sub-topics are not marked separately yet.
A problem is covered only when its key papers were read in full and its open questions are tracked. One paper or one abstract makes it partly covered.
An approach is marked the same way, by what the atlas holds about the method. Its links show the problems it is used on in the field, including problems the atlas has not touched.
The number on a problem counts the sources listed under it. A paper can sit under more than one problem.
The areas, problems and approaches are an AI-drafted outline, not a published taxonomy. Nothing here is reviewed by a person.

approaches.name: Debate
approaches.plain: Two AIs argue opposite sides so that a weaker judge can find the truth.

approaches.name: Amplification and decomposition
approaches.plain: Split a hard task into pieces a person can check, then build the answer back up.

approaches.name: AI critiques and AI feedback
approaches.plain: AI models point out flaws or give feedback in place of human reviewers.

approaches.name: Prover-verifier games
approaches.plain: Train a model to give answers that a weaker checker can verify.

approaches.name: Weak-to-strong training
approaches.plain: Train a strong model with labels from a weaker supervisor and measure what carries over.

approaches.name: Oversight experiments and benchmarks
approaches.plain: Studies and benchmarks that test whether an oversight method works.

approaches.name: RLHF and reward models
approaches.plain: Train a reward model on human preferences, then train the AI to score well on it.

approaches.name: Training on written principles
approaches.plain: Train models or safeguards against a written list of rules.

approaches.name: Model organisms
approaches.plain: Deliberately build misaligned models to study a risk safely.

approaches.name: Probing and representation reading
approaches.plain: Read concepts, such as what the model takes to be true, directly from its internal activity.

approaches.name: Sparse autoencoders
approaches.plain: Break a model's internal activity into many sparse, readable features.

approaches.name: Red teaming
approaches.plain: People or AIs attack a system on purpose to find its failures.

approaches.name: AI monitors
approaches.plain: One model watches another's actions or reasoning and flags danger.

approaches.name: Machine-checked proofs
approaches.plain: Proofs checked line by line by the Lean proof assistant.

approaches.name: Information theory
approaches.plain: Measuring how much a judge or monitor can learn from what it sees.

approaches.name: Singular learning theory
approaches.plain: Track what a model learns through the shape of its loss landscape.

approaches.name: Cryptography
approaches.plain: Use cryptography to hide, or to prove, properties of a model.

approaches.name: Game theory
approaches.plain: Model AI interactions as games with incentives.

approaches.name: Activation steering
approaches.plain: Change a model's behaviour by editing its internal activity directly.

approaches.name: Pretraining data curation
approaches.plain: Filter what a model learns from in the first place, for example to leave out weapons knowledge.

changelog.change: First draft: 12 areas, 54 sub-areas, marked against the atlas at da24e54.

Restructured into three levels after review: 11 research areas, 49 research problems and 18 approaches. Debate and other methods became approaches linked to the problems they serve, so no area counts as covered yet.

Added 2 areas (Societal resilience; Societal impacts and ethics, scope to confirm), 34 problems, 2 approaches and sub-topic lists, after checking the 2026 Singapore Consensus and the MIT AI Risk Repository. Evaluation became Evaluation and risk assessment; systemic effects moved to Societal resilience.
Kept Societal impacts and ethics as an area, by the maintainer's choice on the decision card.
